newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices tumble as strike ends.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices tumble as strike ends.

text.p: Coffee prices tumbled Tuesday as a week-old strike ended in Colombia and sparked a wave of profit-taking by speculators.

After soaring last week to the highest level in almost two years, prices weakened from the outset after union leaders and government officials reached a deal to end the strike in Colombia, the world's second largest producer.
"The market was overbought and the end of the strike gave speculators another reason to take profits," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt.

Coffee for May delivery fell 9.75 cents to 157.25 cents a pound at the Coffee, Sugar, and Cocoa Exchange in New York. The May contract hit a high of 172.25 cents on Friday, capping a 70 percent climb during a two month run-up.
"Basically this is the first major correction the market has made," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "After the dramatic move we have had, I would not expect anything less."
Corn prices rose sharply boosted by heavy buying by investment funds.

"It was huge fund buying, somewhere between 80 million and 100 million bushels," said Paul Hagens, vice president for Chicago-based trade house FIMAT Futures. "Funds reversed positions, they were short and are going long."

Dealers also said a cattle report issued late on Friday by the U.S. Department of Agriculture bolstered prices. It showed there was a sharp increase in the number of cattle placed on feed in the leading states during January. Corn is a major cattle feed.
"The early gains in corn off the cattle numbers took us into buy stops that rallied the whole floor," said Mark Cermak of Chicago trade house O'Connor and Co.
March corn rose 8-3/4 cents to $2.82-3/4 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade after hitting $2.83, its highest level in almost four months.
The strength of corn prices prompted buying in other pits and March wheat added 4-3/4 cents to $3.64-1/4 a bushel and March soybeans jumped 18 cents to $7.79 a bushel.
Heating oil fell amid forecasts for higher-than-normal temperatures in the Northeast, the world's largest market for heating oil, when stocks are more than ample at the tail end of the winter season.

"The weather is expected to be warmer here and for the rest of the world for that matter, and the warmer weather has been creating a surfeit," said Pat Hughes, market analyst with Chevron Corp in Walnut Creek, California.
March heating oil fell 1.39 cents to 59.42 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange, after falling as low as 58.50 cents, the lowest level in seven months.
Weather Services Corp. said temperatures will run well above normal this week in the northeastern United States.
March crude oil managed small gains, rising 11 cents to $22.52 a barrel, while March gasoline lost 0.09 cent to 64.16 cents a gallon.
